newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Economists see Swedish price fall shortlived.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Economists see Swedish price fall shortlived.

text.p: Sweden posted price falls for the second consecutive month on Thursday with a lower-than-expected consumer price figure (CPI) for November but economists saw the price falls as temporary.
Consumer prices slipped 0.3 percent in November from October giving an annualised fall of 0.3 percent. The market had expected a 0.1 percent dip, according to a Reuters poll.

But economists said the falls, the first seen in Sweden for 37 years, were temporary, pointing to underlying inflation of 0.7 percent in October and forecasting inflation, albeit low, from January next year.
"We should see positive figures in January, but inflation is likely to remain below one percent until next summer," Bengt Hansson, senior economist at Handelsbanken, told Reuters.
The trend began in October when Sweden's Central Statistics Bureau (SCB) reported unchanged CPI giving a price fall of 0.1 percent compared with 2.7 percent inflation a year earlier.
The SCB attributed the fall in November mainly to lower mortgage rates and lower value added tax (VAT) on food that took effect in January this year.
But as the effect of the VAT cut will cease on January 1, 1997, economists expected inflation to resume after a third month of price falls in December.

Sweden's CPI is unique as it includes mortgage interest rates and 1.2 percentage points of the November downturn stemmed from lower interest rates following the Riksbank's aggressive rate cutting this year.
"The main reason for the drop in consumer prices is falling interest rates, which are good for the economy," Olle Djerf, economist at banking group Nordbanken, told Reuters.
Some economists argue that a few months of falling prices could more firmly establish Sweden as a country with low inflation, which in turn could prompt interest rates to fall further.
"It will help establish Sweden as a low-inflation country with a long-term low inflation and low wage increases," Hansson said.
The central bank's (Riksbank) inflation target is two percent with a flexibility of one percentage point either way.

"During periods of slow economic growth, inflation should be allowed to be lower than two percent and in periods with strong economic trends it should be allowed to be higher than two percent," said Djerf, dismissing any negative effects of the current figures.
Djerf forecast inflation will rise to two percent at the end of next year with 1997 inflation averaging one percent.

Economists said the continuing low inflationary figures boded well for further cuts to the Riksbank's key interest rate, the repo rate which began the year at 8.91 percent but now stands at 4.35 percent.
Many economists expect the Riksbank to lower the repo rate further, forecasting it will bottom out at below four percent.
The November figure underpinned expectations for another cut next Tuesday when the Riksbank will also present its last inflation report for the year.
"We expect the Riksbank to respond (to CPI figures) by cutting the repo rate by 25 basis points to 4.10 percent next Tuesday," James Mckay at Painewebber said in a statement.
